utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the interpreters. Good afternoon to Defence and Prosecution counsel and to the accused. We can now proceed with Witness DO. Yes, DO. All right, Witness DO should be brought into the court, but that witness is covered by protective measures, I am saying this for the public, because part of his identity is going to be distorted. Have the witness brought in, but be sure that the curtains are drawn before having done so. All right. The witness can be brought in now. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The curtains can be raised now. Do you hear me, Witness DO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Please be seated. Were you able to rest? I don't dare say, "Did you relax," but at least have you rested a bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you feel all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you continue your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We thank you for that. Let me remind you that you are still under oath and that this is the direct examination, that is, the part of the trial which is conducted by the Defence counsel. You are protected. Your face does not appear on the screen. As I said, you have been covered by protective measures. You are under the protection of the Tribunal. You can speak without fear. Let me also speak to the public. I know that frequently academicians follow what we do. I'd like to say good afternoon to those people as well, but I would also like to say that certain testimonies and certain evidence will be extremely difficult to hear. I say this for the attention of the public gallery in case you would not be able to bear that kind of testimony. Having said so, Mr. Nobilo, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I should like to say that the photograph we had previously when we completed our examination on Monday afternoon shall be placed on the ELMO once again. It is a horrible photograph showing half the body of the husband of our witness. I would like to ask you to turn the photograph around where the upper half of the body can be seen which has been cut in two, and you can see the spine partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DO, we go back to this horrible event, unhappy event. When were you delivered this body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: On the 21st of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you heard from a woman? Was your husband killed in the fighting? Was he arrested? What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: My husband was arrested, taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: (redacted). They took the aunt away to Zenica, and my husband, they kept my husband. There were some rumours circulating that my husband was arrested, but on the 21st of January, I came to ascertain whether it was my husband or not. I did not have the courage to go and identify the body, and his father went, my father-in-law, in fact, to go and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I am going to object. This line of question was covered at the conclusion of the last session. We are repeating rather graphic testimony that I think is unnecessary. It does not add additional facts. We had, as I say, this testimony previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I feel, Mr. Nobilo, that this has been spoken about. This is a particularly cruel event for the witness. Perhaps you could ask your question a different way, with a different objective, or else don't ask it and move onto something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree, but it is quite a new thing that the witness heard that her husband was taken prisoner alive, and another piece of information that the witness heard, I would like it to be entered into the transcript, the manner in which the Muslims proceeded and what they did to her husband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do to your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: I heard that he was placed on a stick, impaled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that tradition in Bosnia, this impalement tradition in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Well, when the Turks ruled over Bosnia, this kind of thing was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now going to show you some photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we are preparing this material, it is a photographic report composed by the police station in Vitez, and I should like to avoid showing the first page of this photographic report because you will be able to see the village we are talking about, so if we leave out the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D457.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So do not display page 1, please, but page 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DO --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Nobilo, could you wait until we get a copy of the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Okay, sorry, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you are the judge of your own strategy. Is it absolutely indispensable, to show all these photos? I do not want to rule for you, and, of course, the Rules allow us to do it, but, of course, I do not want to make use of those powers. The decision is ultimately yours, but try to make sure that this is not gone into in overly great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President. After the photographs, the point concerns the second part of the body of Witness DO's husband that we wish to show. But I would like to say something regarding this witness and the witnesses this week and, perhaps, later on. We are going to see a lot of brutalities, a lot of blood, a lot of atrocities and horrors, but the Defence feels it is necessary for the Trial Chamber to see this to understand the conditions under which General Blaskic had to act and to realise that people become vindictive after horrors of this kind and that this leads on to the chain of terror and vindictiveness, and we don't take pleasure in looking at photographs of this kind either, but terror breeds terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this conduct which is reprehensible took place, I am told from the previous testimony, January 9th, 1994, and its relevancy is considerably attenuated given the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I believe that the indictment, the second amended indictment, was something that I checked on the other day when the witness began the testimony. In the second indictment, it goes up to January 1994. You did not specify anything further than that; do we agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, and that applies to the persecution count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are really going to the furthest extremes of the indictment here, the furthest limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This is one in a series of unfortunate and continuing incidents which we think are important. We'll withdraw it if January 1994 is to be stricken from the indictment. We will withdraw the testimony of this witness if it is outside the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. These points have been underscored. Continue, Mr. Nobilo, but with all the legal and factual warnings that we have indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. So we are ready at any time to withdraw if the date -- but for the moment, this is covered by the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DO, do you recognise Drazen on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: (No translation).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to turn to the one but last photograph now which is marked number 3. Utanda Drazenko is on this photograph, and the witness recognised him. It wasn't entered into the transcript. So the one but last photograph of this photographic report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Drazenko Utanda, could you tell us who that is, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Drazen Utanda was there with us. He is from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No, he is not a Croat. He is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he live in the same village that you lived in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The one but last photograph, please. Witness DO, can you see, and you can look on the original photograph, whether you recognise this portion of the body? What is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can look at the original photograph on that apparatus there, on the ELMO. Show it to the witness, please. Take a look at the picture, the original photo. Could you tell us into the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: That is the lower half of my husband's body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that lower half?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe what this represents, what part of the body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Well, it is from the waist down. The legs, I recognise them. I recognise the socks, the tracksuit. I saw that with my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, please, at the time you left your husband, did he have any weapons in the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No, he had no weapons in the house. He was not able to walk. He was on crutches, and he was not military-able. Had he been so, he would not have been in the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you enumerate all the victims in the village in which you lived, the ones that you can remember at the present time? So don't tell us the name of your husband, just say "my husband," but do you know any other individuals who were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Dragan Vidovic, Miro Vidovic, Drazen Vidovic, Ankica Vidovic, Ankica Grbavac, Nikola Jankovic, Petar Petkovic, Drazen Utanda, and Zvonko Santic. I don't know any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Stjepan Ramljak was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, Stjepan Ramljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a two-year-old child killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Danijel Grbavac was a two-year-old child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the brother of Nevenka Buhic die?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: He was wounded, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were eight soldiers killed belonging to the Munja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, they were below the house where I lived. That's where they were located. They slept there, and they were caught while they were still in bed, and I only know that that is where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court whether there were other victims but that you cannot recall their names at this present time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. There were others, but I don't know their names. I was given a drip, an infusion. It was difficult for me at that time, and it is always very difficult for me. A lot of pain was inflicted on me and my children, and it will last throughout our lives, and probably I can't remember everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether these people resisted or were they surprised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No, these young men were sleeping, as far as I know, down there, and as far as we were able to see on the tapes, they were even tied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to show a video now. It is a BBC video from the village in which Witness DO lived, and after we have been shown the video, I have two or three more questions to ask her in connection with the video. May we have the lights dimmed as well, please? We haven't got the picture yet. No videotape yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you stop it, please? We do not have any image.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is a slight technical problem. It won't take too long to fix it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We can proceed. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we repeat the central part of the tape which was crucial? It was nighttime, that is to say, it was dark. It was filmed in the basement, but you will be able to see that the hands of the people there were tied. So may we ask our technical service to go back to that central part of the tape, and this can be seen very well on the original tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until then, I am going to ask you, Madam, whether this is a scene from your village?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the film that we saw was perfectly clear. I don't think there is any need to see it a second time, and I would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The problem is, Mr. President, I viewed the original tape that we gave to the technical unit, and you can see a lot more from the inside of this basement on the original. It has been copied, I think, for purposes of putting it on to a separate tape for an exhibit, but something has happened in the copy, and it is not visible. I don't know if they have the original tape that we tendered and they can locate that portion of that tape, so that at least Your Honours can see it clearly once. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you are entitled to show it a second time. It is legitimate for the parties to show the evidence under the best technical conditions, if possible, even if it is painful. Do you want to continue asking questions while the technical staff prepares the film?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I can, but we just have a short portion of the video to show. But I can go on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not come from an area, from the area where all this happened, you came from elsewhere; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband know any Muslim in the place in which he was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why do you think your husband was so brutally killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Because he is a Croat, nothing else, just because he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May we now see the tape once again, and after that the second part of the tape? And a little more light, if we may have it, please. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Stop. You can continue now, thank you. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We can continue and complete the second portion, the last part of the tape that we haven't seen yet. I would also like to caution the audience that there will be brutal scenes. The next tape comes to us from a private source and shows a body. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your husband, madam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have concluded the examination of this witness with this tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we will now turn to the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Harmon, do you have some questions that you want to ask Witness DO? As you know, I've already told you, the Prosecutor has the right to ask you questions. If you need any assistance -- do you need to rest? Do you need to take a break? Do you want to take a 10-minute break? Because we can suspend the hearing for ten minutes before the Prosecutor asks his questions. Don't hesitate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, we may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, proceed, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness DO. My name is Mark Harmon, and to my right are my colleagues, Mr. Andrew Cayley and Mr. Gregory Kehoe from the Prosecutor's office. I have only a few questions to ask you, and I would like you to, if you get uncomfortable at all or get tired or fatigued or anxious, let me know and we can take a break. I don't want to cause you any further distress than you have already been caused. Let me ask you, first off: The events that you described, if I correctly understood, occurred on the 9th of January in the year of 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to show you Defence Exhibit 455.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that is an exhibit that is under seal, so I assume we have to go into private session to take a look at the exhibit, and I would like to put it on the ELMO. Mr. Dubuisson, will 455 not be shown on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will go into a private session for a few moments. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, we have gone back into public session now. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DO, the nine members of the HVO who lived in the lower part of the house where you and your husband and your family lived, do you know if on January the 9th, 1994 they had weapons in the lower portion of the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from your testimony, I understood that shortly after the attack on the village started you and two of your children immediately fled the house and took refuge some distance away from that location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return to the village, to the location of your former residence at any time prior to the 21st of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did return, and I found my husband, his jacket, rather. I saw it was cut in nine places. I saw that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date when you returned to the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No, no, that was after the burial of the first part of his body, and I can't tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason I ask you that question is, we just had a film that was shown from BBC, and it said that the fighting was taking place in the village, the HVO was attempting to recapture the village, and that that fighting had lasted 12 days. Would it be fair to say that you returned to your village sometime after the 21st of January?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: I did not return in order to live there. I got out with my children. I didn't have a thing. I went back to get some things and the house had already burned down. Downstairs I found two blankets that I had already taken, so I just came by and I saw that. But I went back. I didn't stay there. I didn't go there to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For clarity of the record, Mr. President, the BBC film says it was attempting to retake a village it had lost 12 days before. There wasn't a reference to the fighting in the village, I believe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DO, you listed a number of people you recalled in the village who had been killed, and you gave us a few minutes ago the names of those individuals. My question is: Did you see any of those people killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware there was a considerable combat in your former village where the HVO attempted to and ultimately succeeded in retaking the area where you had lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No, no, I was no longer aware what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Witness DO, thank you very much. Mr. President and Your Honours, I have no additional questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you want to add some clarifications in the redirect, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just two questions. Re-examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DO, the people you enumerated, those who were killed, as you said, were they killed when the Muslims got into your village and killed your husband, or were they killed afterwards when the HVO fought for recapturing the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No, no, this was the morning when everybody was being killed. All of these people were there while I was there. It was hard for me to recognise everyone. Perhaps someone stayed back, some of the people, I couldn't remember, but all the people I mentioned were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor put a question to you establishing that there were soldiers downstairs in your house. Were the eight members of the Munjas in your house or in the neighbouring house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No, no, beneath my house, which was the first next to the house where I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "beneath my house," when you use that expression, you mean the neighbouring house further downhill; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was a bit uphill and this house was a bit downhill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you still maintain that there were no weapons in your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We offer into evidence D455, which is under seal, the map, and D456, which is a photograph, and D457, also a photograph under seal, the first page, rather, is under seal, and then two video clips. We tender all of that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Let me turn to my colleagues. Do you have any questions to add, Judge Riad? Judge Shahabuddeen, no questions? I have no questions, either, to ask you, Witness DO. The registrar is indicating something to me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I want to say the first part of the videotape will be 458A, that is the BBC version, and the other one, the private film, was D458B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness DO, you have shown a great deal of courage, and we thank you for that. Try to go home and to find the peace of mind and the serenity that you need. The Tribunal thanks you. Registrar, what are we going to do now to ensure the protection of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, too, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That depends on whether you want to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we will take a short, ten-minute break, the time necessary to help the witness leave the courtroom. Is the witness protected? Is the next witness protected, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The next witness has similar face and also voice distortion. If you wish we could have that witness seated during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. I suggest that we take a ten-minute break, which will allow Witness DO to leave the courtroom with the protective measures which are extended to her, and then contrary to what we ordinarily do, you will bring in the next witness who will be there when we come back in. All right, the hearing is suspended for about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing now. Have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think this is Witness DP.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Witness DP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness DP, first of all, do you hear me? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing for a moment. I am going to ask you to acknowledge your name on the piece of paper which is being given to you, but don't state your name. We just want to be sure that this is, in fact, you. Would you show the witness the piece of paper with the name? Is that your name? Do not say your name. Is that, in fact, your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Nods)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You are now going to take an oath. I think you are going to say the sentence which you should repeat or you can do it yourself. Please stay standing for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will read the statement and ask the witness to repeat after me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Listen to me, please, the Registrar is going to read you an oath in short bits of sentences. It will be interpreted for you into your own mother tongue, and then you are asked to repeat it, and once that is done, you can sit down. Please proceed. Read slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Try to relax, that's the most important thing. There is no need to be afraid. I know that this is a setting which can be a bit awesome, but you are before Judges and you have nothing to fear. If you have any need at all to stop, don't hesitate to tell us. Take your time, and we can stop. You are under complete protection, and you can now first answer the questions that will be asked by the counsel for the accused who is in this room, that is, General Blaskic, and then you will be asked some questions by the Prosecutor, and finally by the Judges. Are you prepared to begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I wish to suggest that we move into private session for two or three minutes in order to get some identification data from this witness very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Just at the beginning, we will go into a closed session so that any identifying information that you give us will be completely protected, and once that's been done, we can move back into public session. As I told you, the image of your face is distorted on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are still under protective measures. Just don't say the name of your village. Mr. Nobilo, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DO, please, could you just speak a bit louder because I have trouble hearing you. Tell me, your Muslim neighbours, don't mention any names, please, but tell me, did you have any problems? Were there any problems between Croats and Muslims in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now we shall move on to the 24th of April, 1993. Can you explain to the Court how this day began and what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, please do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: With my husband, I was working in the fields; we wanted to plant potatoes. Four neighbours came by, they were Muslims, and they were running towards us, and we asked them what had happened because they had had coffee at our place only a little while before that, and they said, "Nothing happened. We just came here so that nothing would happen." And we said, "What is it?" And they said, "The Mujahedin have gotten out of control, and we came to protect you. Come up there with us," and we all went to the village because there weren't too many of us anyway. There were about 35 of us altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Is it possible for you to speak a bit slower so that the interpreters could precisely interpret what you are saying? So your neighbours said that the Mujahedin got out of control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: And then they said that they came to protect us. We believed them because their sons worked at the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They said that they came to protect you. Were they your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, our neighbours, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Then all of us from the village got together in the middle of the village, and then he took one of our Croats, this neighbour of ours, I mean, this Muslim, and he said that he should go with his brother to go to the command and that they should say that these other people have gotten out of control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, what kind of command are we talking about? What army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: This was the command of the BH army, but the Mujahedin were together with them. They all belonged to the same command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, the command of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Mujahedin, where did they have their headquarters, their command? What's the name of this place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: I know that it was called Mehurici. I only know of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go on. Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Then this man went, and all of a sudden, they showed up in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: The army, the Mujahedin. They were not masked, and the rest were masked. They had socks over their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, these people whom you call Mujahedin who were not masked, what did they look like? Were they different from your Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, they were quite different. They were short, they were dark, and they were there for a year. They wore those long robes in Mehurici. We saw them down there, and we also saw them in Travnik. We saw them all over the place. We knew what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when you say "these long robes," what does that mean? Could you describe this attire to the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: It was white, these white robes. They didn't wear a belt or anything, but these robes were just flowing around them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the garment that they wore, we could call it a shirt, for example, how long was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: It went down to their heels. They had these shirts flowing down to their heels. Those were the guys who didn't go to the frontline, and those who went with the army to the frontline, they were dressed just like the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the colour of their skin differ from that of the local Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did some of them have beards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Some did, others didn't, and then armed Muslims too, those who were younger, they also started dressing the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, these others who had socks over their heads, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: They were dressed in camouflage. They only had these socks on their heads, and when we got in and when we were supposed to run away, we were actually told to get into a house, and not all of us could fit into this house, so the owner of the house locked up his house, and then they tried to attack the house --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. When you say "the owner locked up the house," could you tell us what nationality this owner was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the local population mostly took shelter in that house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, we ran into that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you manage to get into the house or did you stay outside, you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: I got into the house. I managed to get into the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these who were attacking the house, who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: It was the Mujahedin and the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please describe what happened after that? How did they attack the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: They were shooting through the doors, and the owner of the house stood behind the front door, and he was begging them not to shoot. And they threw things into the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: When we got out, we saw that they were throwing something green into the house. The house was in smoke, and the walls were falling off, the ceiling was coming down. It was foggy. We couldn't even see each other. We were all in one room and then in another room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. When they would throw this green thing into the kitchen, did it explode?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can we describe this green thing? Was it a bomb? Do you know what a bomb is, a grenade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yeah, I know what a grenade is, but I didn't really see this thing. I didn't see it then. I saw the smoke, though, and when they threw us out of the house, then I saw what they were doing. They were unscrewing this thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the kitchen where they threw this explosive device, were there people in this kitchen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened after the owner of the house begged them not to shoot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Then they broke down the door, and he had a rifle in his hands, and he shot immediately, and he killed one of them, and then they killed him. And then they barged into the third room with rifles, and this was a Mujahedin who had barged in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, this house that they barged into, how many people were there in there? How many people took shelter in this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Well, there were only about ten of us in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in addition to the owner of the house who shot in the hallway when they broke in, did anybody else have weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No, nobody else had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all the rest of you civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, we were all civilians. UNPROFOR took pictures of the dead bodies, and everybody wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say that the owner of the house hit a man, shot a man. Could you describe him, what he looked like and what he had on his head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: He had some kind of a cap on. He was dark, he was short, he had nothing on his face, he had a rifle, and he tried to throw us out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the man who tried to throw you out. Did you see the man whom the owner of the house, the Croat, had shot, had killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Well, we went by Stipe in the hallway, and this man was lying there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a Croat; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Croat. And then we went out, and the first neighbour was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that it was your neighbour who was killed? How come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Well, we know. The Croat neighbour of mine was very young when I got married. I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the member of the BH army who was killed? What did he look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Well, he's the one I told you about, the Bosnia-Herzegovina man. I told you what he was like. He wore camouflage clothes, like the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this member of the BH army, the Muslim who wore camouflage clothes, did he have a sock over his head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, but they took off this sock because they tried to save his life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they took off this sock, did you recognise him then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, I did recognise him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise him as being your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Then they kicked us out, and then the one who had gone to the command, to the headquarters, came back, I mean, both of them came back, and they wanted to kill them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who wanted to kill who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: The Mujahedin wanted to kill the guy who went to headquarters and this other Croat of ours, these two, when they were going back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who went to the command, a Croat and a Muslim from your village; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then they came back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, and then they came back. And they rushed towards them. They wanted to kill them. The Muslim stretched his hands out and he said, "What do you want? I'm a Muslim brother." And they said to him, "Well, you're a Muslim brother, what are you doing here?" And they told both of them to go where they had come from. One of these men with a sock on his head raced out as soon as he saw them and said, "This Croat should come back. This is not a Muslim brother. He's not a Muslim brother. Let him come back."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, how many civilians were there in this village of yours? How many Croat villagers, civilians who were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Thirty-four of us were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: And then this Croat came back, and then they tied him up too. They tied up all of us with a rope. So they tied him up too, and they said, they said he should be tied even harder. They took a rope with which they tie hay and they tied him with this rope, and they hit them with rifle butts, and they kicked them and they made them kneel. And then our people begged them to stop, because they couldn't kneel while they were tied. One neighbour came, brought a car, and he did not have a mask, and he brought a full Toyota, full of Mujahedin, and then they told us to get up and they made us walk in front of them, to walk two-by-two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all of you go? Did the men also go and did the women and children stay behind, or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: I thought that all of us were going. We were imprisoned until 11.30, and then they let us go. They said, "Go ahead, there is a bus waiting for you. Go back to your homes." We had set out, and then when we got into the bus I was looking around because I wanted to see where my husband was, and I had my child with me. When I got into the bus I saw that my husband was not there. I thought that he was there where they had separated us, women one side, men on the other side, because they had locked us up in the cellar. We were taken prisoner. And the Mujahedin lived upstairs above us. And the men were locked up in the shed, and when we got into the bus I saw that my husband wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was missing of the men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: When I started to cry and shout, I thought that my husband was still in the shed and that we had left, and my neighbour cried out to me that three others were missing, as well. My husband and the other men remained dead in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask where the men were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, we asked them. They said, "You must not worry. Don't be afraid. They will be exchanged." Then they took us away. There were two other Serb women with us and two Serb men, and we were separated there. They were left in the school, and they took us further away to our houses, and that's where we stayed. We asked them once again and pleaded with them to tell us where the others were, and they said that they had gone to be exchanged. The next day we asked them again, and pleaded with them again, and they told us that in the course of the day they would tell us where they had gone to be exchanged. UNPROFOR turned up then and went up towards our village. We asked them to release us. They did not do this, and they told us, "Flee to the basement because the Mujahedin are coming to slaughter you." And we were sent down into a basement, and then let us go. And later on UNPROFOR arrived and we were able to go out of the basement towards UNPROFOR. From an armed vehicle, one armoured vehicle, one of our Croats peeked through, put his head through, and told us that our menfolk had been killed. Once again we asked and implored them to let us go to the village to see where our menfolk were, but they didn't allow us to do this. We spent the night there, once again, and in the morning we got up and there was nobody anywhere to be seen. One by one, we went through the wood and came to our village and we found our men there in one house. They were lined up and covered with blankets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many bodies were there? How many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Five men were killed. And I asked to see -- and I asked him -- and he hugged me, and he said, "I wanted to see father." He asked me to let him go and find his father, and I let him do this. And when we started uncovering the bodies I saw a man lying on his back. The second body was uncovered and they were turned -- their faces were turned to the floor. I saw one man, that he had been slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that he was slaughtered from the back, from the top, how did you see the head severed from the body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: From the backside, from the back. I saw this from the back. He had been slaughtered, and the head was separated, severed from the neck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the head was separated from the neck and body. How many centimetres was it severed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: About five centimetres, but I didn't see that it was cut off entirely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't seen the throat side, you didn't see the side of the throat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No, the head was turned, the face was downward, so I couldn't see the face. I just saw the back of the neck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the people tell you later on who buried the bodies? Was the head completely cut off from the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: People said that my husband's head was completely cut off. I saw that he was slaughtered. I saw that all of them had been slaughtered, that their throats had been -- and that their sexual organs had been cut off and their arms and legs had been broken. And they told me that my husband had a television on his head, and that that's how they found him when UNPROFOR came. And that they had to eat, they were told to eat flowers from the window, and weeds. That's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness DP, tell the Court, please, who told you that one of the bodies the head had been severed from the body, that the sex organs had been cut off and the hands and legs had been broken? Who told you that? Don't tell us the name, but describe to us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Our man told us, one of ours, because we asked them, we asked them -- we brought clothes for them to change their clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in keeping with Croatian conditions you wanted to put clean clothes on the dead men, and what did the man tell you who tried to change their clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: He said it was impossible to unclothe them because everything had been separated and if he were to take the clothes off, the whole body would disintegrate into pieces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of these five bodies, one was a neighbour who was killed in the house before your eyes who was in the hallway protecting his own home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other four bodies, the other four men, did you see them taken alive, arrested alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that with my very own eyes. I prayed to God that they had killed me then, rather than seeing what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, later on did you see a photograph with somebody's heart being plucked out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a picture of this where, a body with a heart plucked out, and this could be seen from the clothing. And it exists today, but I don't know who has that particular photograph, but I saw it in a shop window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your husband's heart taken out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: No, my neighbour's, but I did not see my husband. I don't know if I will ever see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next? When you had seen this massacre, what did the Croat civilians do? Did they remain in the village? Did you stay in the village or go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: UNPROFOR came on that day and we asked them to take us away. We stood in front of UNPROFOR and UNPROFOR told us that they had come to the scene but not to -- to do an examination on the scene but not to take civilians away. We cried and said we wanted to leave and said we didn't dare stay anymore, and they took us halfway, and that's where they left us. The BiH army did not allow us to pass through. There were negotiations with UNPROFOR, and I heard that they asked UNPROFOR for ten tons of flour and then they would release us and our dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you heard a condition was being stipulated for an exchange of you and the dead bodies, that they were offering ten tons of flour; did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, we heard that they asked for ten tons of flour. We were there at 2 a.m.. They did not allow us free passage, and what UNPROFOR discussed with them -- but they left us, anyway, and returned the bodies on the next day. But they didn't send the bodies to us, but they allowed the bodies to be taken for burial from the place they had expelled us Croats. I wasn't able to go there. I only went there later on for -- later on, when there was security in the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us when the Croat civilians from your place started downhill towards the territory under control of the HVO, is it true that you went to Bila then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, we came at midnight to Bila. We were taken there by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Bila was controlled by the Croats; was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you put up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: We were put up in a school, and a woman took us in her own house, and then we were put up there in that building, in the same building that I live today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a school building, the school building in Bila. Did you come from your village? Were you the only one, or did a number of Croats go down towards the northern reaches to the enclave controlled --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Not on that occasion, only my village. But later on in June, I don't exactly know what date it was, but Bukovica, Radonjici, Vucja Gora, Maljine, Susanj, Ovljau, Brakovici, Cuklje, all those were taken to Bila in one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means that the Croats left all these places; does it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, the Croats left these places, because they had to at gunpoint. They were expelled at gunpoint. And a mother threw her dead child into the bushes to save her head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are now going to see a video, and while we look at this video I'm going to ask you a few questions. May we see the video and have the lights dimmed, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this scenery, this panorama? Have a good look at the whole video, first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are those the villages that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The smoke we see, what is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Those are the houses burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Croat houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that took place in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but I don't remember the exact date. I know this woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She is from Maljine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all these neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, these neighbours are from my parish. We used to go to church together. Not from my village, but from my parish, that's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this in front of the school building in Bila?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, and I live there today. This is the truck and they are unloading and loading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this what it looked like when the people arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fleeing in the face of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes. All these people fled during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at dawn they came to this place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, they arrived throughout the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area where your villages are located, are they at an altitude higher up in the hills?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the refugees had to move down the hill towards the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, can you go back to your parish? The parishioners of these ten villages, is it possible for the Croatians to return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it's possible for us to return. We would all like to return, but we're all afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us, what about the houses, have they been destroyed, the houses of your parish?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, they have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were burned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, they burned to the ground. There were refugees in my house, and then the refugees left and when they did so the house was set fire to and it burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This all happened in June 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, this completes our examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. As I said to you, Witness DP, the Prosecutor is going to ask you a few questions, and then the Judges. Mr. Cayley, will you be conducting the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I only have a couple of comments to make, actually, Mr. President, if we could go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes? All right we're going to go into a closed session to hear Mr. Cayley's comments. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 4.43 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday 24 the 10th day of December, 1998 at10.00 a.m.
